claim: The note teaches that お is used almost only on things belonging to the listener or a third person, which the book does not say and which is false as a general rule.
evidence: Book NOTES: 'The prefix お is added to the word くに to specify the country or birthplace of the person you are talking to.' Card note: 'It's used almost entirely for things belonging to the person you're talking to (or a third person), not your own things'. The card's own hint names みやげ, whose usual form おみやげ carries お with no sense of 'yours'.
fix: Limit the note to what the book says: お on くに makes it the listener's country, and drop the 'almost entirely' generalisation.

claim: The hint on the Production front illustrates お with two words the learner has not been taught.
evidence: Card hint: 'the prefix on native words like なまえ (namae, "name") and みやげ (miyage, "souvenir")'. Neither なまえ nor みやげ is in chapter-0 or this chapter; the book's only example here is おくに.
fix: Replace the hint with one built on this chapter's word, e.g. 'the prefix that turns くに into the listener's country'.

claim: The card introduces someone with こちらは but leaves さん off the name, against the book's rule and every introduction it prints.
evidence: Book: こちら 'this one (polite for "this person")'; KS3 'こちらは のぞみデパートの たなかさんです'; Exercise V 'こちらは ベルリンモーターズの ホフマンさんです'; NOTES 'さん ... cannot be used after one's own name'. Card: 'こちらはイギリスのライアンです' / 'This is Ryan from England'.
fix: Add さん (こちらはイギリスのライアンさんです), or if it is meant as self-identification, rewrite it without こちらは.

claim: The English renders イギリス as England, where the book glosses it as the United Kingdom.
evidence: Book WORD POWER vocabulary: 'イギリス United Kingdom'. Deck card igirisu: 'United Kingdom'. Card irl-l1-28: 'This is Ryan from England'.
fix: Change the English to 'from the United Kingdom' (or 'from the UK').

claim: The English renders イギリスじん as English, where the book and this deck's own card say British.
evidence: Book GRAMMAR 2: 'いいえ、イギリスじんです。 No, (he is) British.' Deck card igirisujin: 'British (person)'. Card irl-l1-27: 'ライアンさんはイギリスじんですか？' / 'Is Ryan English?'.
fix: Change the English to 'Is Ryan-san British?'.

claim: The target ends in a full-width question mark after か, which the book never writes.
evidence: Book: 'スミスさんは アメリカじんですか。' (か questions end in 。). Card target: 'ジャックさんはフランスじんですか？'. Every other question card in this chapter ends in か with no mark.
fix: Drop the trailing ？ from the target.

claim: The target ends in a full-width question mark after か, which the book never writes.
evidence: Book: 'スミスさんは イギリスじんですか。' Card target: 'ライアンさんはイギリスじんですか？'.
fix: Drop the trailing ？ from the target.

claim: The note writes せんせい in kanji, which a learner of this kana edition cannot read.
evidence: Book: the kana edition writes everything in kana; no kanji is taught by this chapter. Card note: '(e.g. saying 先生 to or about them instead of their name)'.
fix: Write せんせい (sensei) in the note instead of 先生.

claim: The book's second use of よろしく おねがいします and its gloss of よろしく are on no card.
evidence: Book NOTES: 'It is also used when taking one's leave after having asked a favor. よろしく means "well" and is used as a request for the other person's favorable consideration in the future.' Card note covers only the introduction use.
fix: Add a sentence to the note: also said when leaving after asking a favour; よろしく means 'well'.

claim: The book's points that さん is used for any gender and with either surname or given name are on no card.
evidence: Book NOTES: 'さん is used regardless of gender and can be used with both the last name and the given name. In business situations, "last name + さん" is the most common'. Card note: 'Suffix — attaches after a person's name; cannot be used after one's own name'.
fix: Add to the note: any gender, surname or given name, surname most common at work.

claim: The note gives a reason for Tanaka omitting his company that the book does not give.
evidence: Book TARGET DIALOGUE prints 'はじめまして。たなかです。' with no comment. Card note: 'Tanaka drops the company here because Smith had already named it when asking for him.'
fix: Drop the second sentence of the note, or soften it to 'the company can be left out once it is known'.
